question.worked_solution:
Let $u=1+x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that $x=u-1.$

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $1$ | $2$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}x{(1+x)}^{4}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(u-1){u}^{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({u}^{5}-{u}^{4})\,\text{d}u \\  & ={(\frac{1}{6}{u}^{6}-\frac{1}{5}{u}^{5})|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}({2}^{6}-{1}^{6})-\frac{1}{5}({2}^{5}-{1}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(64-1)-\frac{1}{5}(32-1) \\  & =\frac{63}{6}-\frac{31}{5} \\  & =\frac{21}{2}-\frac{31}{5} \\  & =\frac{43}{10}\end{aligned}
$$
